Welcome back! Today: how the model is trained. First, a quick review from [last session](wiki:session/2026-01-06).

:::question
In attention, what are the three vectors each token produces, and what is each one for?
:::
Query is what it looks for, key is what it gets matched on. And value is... the score?

note: q and k right; value confused with the score

text:
Close: q and k are right, but the value is **what gets handed over**, not the score. The score is q · k ([see here](msg:2026-01-06.5)).

# 6.1 Training objective: cross-entropy loss

Training text supplies the right next token at every position. The model is graded on the probability {{p|p}} it gave to that correct token:

$$\k{loss}{\mathcal{L}} = -\log \k{p}{p_{\text{correct}}}$$

This is the [cross-entropy loss](term:cross-entropy loss). Some values:

| {{p|p}} | {{loss|loss}} |
|---|---|
| 0.9 | 0.11 |
| 0.5 | 0.69 |
| 0.1 | 2.30 |
| 0.01 | 4.61 |

```viz bars
{ title: "prediction after *the river*", items: [
    { label: "bank", value: 0.55, key: "p" }, { label: "flows", value: 0.25 },
    { label: "money", value: 0.05 }, { label: "other", value: 0.15 } ], format: "pct",
  caption: "Correct token: *bank*. Loss = −log 0.55 ≈ 0.6." }
```

:::question
Why is −log p a better thing to minimise than just (1 − p)? Think about what happens when the model is confidently wrong.
:::
With 1 - p, being at 0.01 or at 0.0001 costs about the same, so the model is not pushed hard when it is very wrong. -log p goes to infinity, so confident mistakes get punished much more.

Exactly right.

# 6.2 Gradient descent

The loss is a function of all the weights. The gradient says, for each weight, which direction makes the loss go up; we step the other way, scaled by the [learning rate](term:learning rate):

```python
for batch in data:
    loss = cross_entropy(model(batch.inputs), batch.targets)
    grads = backprop(loss)          # one number per weight
    for w, g in zip(weights, grads):
        w -= lr * g
```

Toy version: one weight, loss $(w - 2)^2$, start at $w = -3$. Slide the {{learning rate|lr}} and see how fast (or whether) it converges:

```viz plot
{ x: [0, 20], y: [0, 30],
  fns: [{ f: "25 * pow(1 - 2*lr, 2*x)", label: "loss after x steps", key: "lr" }],
  sliders: [{ name: "lr", label: "learning rate", min: 0.01, max: 1.05, value: 0.1, step: 0.01 }],
  caption: "Above 0.5 each step overshoots to the other side; above 1.0 it diverges." }
```

:::question
What goes wrong if the learning rate is far too large? And far too small?
:::
Too large and every step overshoots the minimum, it bounces around or blows up. Too small and it is stable but takes forever to get anywhere.

reason: explains both failure modes, matched the toy

text: You mentioned a KV cache last time. What is that, briefly?

Short version, since it's on the list for later ([4.4](skill:4.4)):

When generating, the model produces one token at a time. Each new token needs q · k against **every earlier token's** key, and their values. Those keys and values never change once computed (earlier tokens can't see later ones), so the model keeps them in memory: that's the [KV cache](term:KV cache). Each step then only computes q, k, v for the one new token.

:::note
The cache grows with every token, per layer and per head, which is why long contexts are memory-hungry. Where it sits: [map](map:kvcache).
:::
